reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an unusually high recurring profit claim for a PancakeSwap bot and instructs viewers to deploy it and deposit funds into its contract. It describes automated trading, a claimed 90% transfer back to the wallet, 10% retention in the protocol, and encourages larger deposits for a claimed 250~300% better return, supported by reported past earnings and deployment and wallet-authorization interfaces. The contract, performance, transfers, losses, and claimed outcomes are not verified.

citations.quote: FREE PancakeSwap Bot | EASY 10x profit EVERY DAY
Deposit funds to exact your newly BOT contract address
After the transaction is confirmed, Start the BOT by clicking the "Action" button
So we're going to send some funds to that contract that we just created.
it will find the liquidity, buy into that project.

opening.argument: The presentation includes concrete risk qualifications that are inconsistent with treating the outcome as certain. It warns that users may fail to fund enough for gas and burn fees, explains that token burns can reduce the amount available, and says the bot works properly only with a recommended minimum balance. Those qualifications frame the result as dependent on costs, token conditions, and available funds rather than as an unconditional payout. The description also says the bot continues until the user activates the Action function, leaving the user control over when the process runs.

citations.quote: I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.
If it targets tokens with 10% burn, that's another 0.04 BNB taken off of 0.4 BNB.
Less than 0.4 BNB doesn't give you much to work with.
The remaining pool keeps front running for profit, until you transaction "Action" function in Remix.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing case emphasizes the headline and funding instructions, but those do not by themselves establish deception. The same material expressly discusses gas fees, burn fees, and the amount needed to operate, while the Action step is presented as a user-controlled trigger. A claimed result may be exaggerated or unverified without making every risk-qualified tutorial a scam.

After the transaction is confirmed, Start the BOT by clicking the "Action" button
I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Mentioning operating costs does not neutralize the central inducement. The title presents an “EASY 10x profit EVERY DAY” claim, while the instructions still tell viewers to deposit funds and start the bot. The gas and burn discussion explains how much money to provide; it does not show that the promised returns are realistic, that the contract is safe, or that any viewer received the described payout.

opening.argument: The video's observable structure is a programming and blockchain operational demonstration. It walks through creating a contract file, compiling Solidity, connecting Remix to an injected Web3 wallet, deploying the contract, and inspecting the deployed address. The visual material likewise shows a Remix coding and deployment interface and a blockchain explorer page. That is consistent with teaching viewers how a smart-contract workflow operates, even if the presenter also describes expected performance. Demonstrating a technical procedure does not itself certify the strategy or guarantee its success.

citations.quote: This is where we're going to be building our contract
this was built with Pragma solidity 6.6
So we're going to deploy this to our wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing case treats the tutorial's operational steps as proof of solicitation, but deployment instructions are also what a technical demonstration requires. Showing a contract, a compiler, a wallet connection, and an explorer page establishes a workflow, not that the presenter has verified the advertised return or that the workflow is fraudulent. The performance language can be understood as the demonstrator's claim, not independent certification.

citations.quote: Then you just follow over to Remix, which is where the window I've started up is right now.
it compiled. So we're going to deploy this to our wallet.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not change what the tutorial tells viewers to do. It directs them to fund a newly created contract and describes pressing Action to engage automated buying and selling. The coding screens show only that code and interfaces exist; they do not establish that the code performs profitable trades, that funds return to the wallet, or that the promised mechanism works.

opening.argument: The supplied material shows a software and smart-contract service workflow, not the usual hallmarks of a credential-harvesting scheme. The stated setup uses MetaMask, Remix, Solidity compilation, deployment, and a contract address; the wallet interface is shown in the context of a transaction. The instructions do not ask viewers to surrender a password or seed phrase, and the materials do not establish a downline or referral-income structure. Whatever one thinks of the trading claims, the presented mechanism is an ordinary technical service interaction whose safety and profitability still require independent evaluation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing case identifies deposits and automated trading, but those are the advertised service's operating steps, not evidence of a hidden credential request or an income chain. The supplied material shows a contract deployment and wallet transaction interface, while the critique itself concedes that the contract, transfers, losses, and outcomes are unverified. Lack of verification is a reason for caution, not proof that the presentation is a scam.

citations.quote: So we're going to send some funds to that contract that we just created.
it will find the liquidity, buy into that project.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The issue is not limited to passwords, seed phrases, or downlines. The video combines a “FREE” high-return headline with instructions to deploy and fund a contract, then claims automated returns to the wallet. A technical interface can make a transaction look legitimate without proving what the contract does or establishing that the promised return exists.
